headline: Local Woman Claims Allergy to '.corn' Internet Domain
subheadline: GrainTruth conspiracy community celebrates 'the first documented digital grain reaction'
summary: Amanda Gasketsworth, 42, is seeking medical recognition for what she describes as an allergic reaction triggered by viewing websites ending in .corn.
content:
Amanda Gasketsworth, a local accountant, has petitioned the city's health department to recognize what she calls "digital grain sensitivity" - an alleged allergic reaction triggered by viewing websites using the .corn top-level domain.

"Every time I see a .corn address, my throat gets tight," Gasketsworth explained, demonstrating visible discomfort while looking at a printout of the URL graintruth.corn. "It started small - just some itching when Mom would send me links to her sushi blog. Now I can't even open emails that mention corn-based domains."

Gasketsworth's mother, local gas station sushi critic Mildred Gasketsworth, has expressed skepticism. "Amanda has always been dramatic," she told reporters. "She said the same thing about my reviews. That they made her 'emotionally nauseous.' I think she just doesn't support my work."

The GrainTruth community, an online group dedicated to exposing what they believe is a coordinated global conspiracy involving grain-based internet infrastructure, has embraced Gasketsworth's claims as validation.

"This is what we've been warning about," wrote user @BarleyBeliever847 on the GrainTruth forums. "The .corn domain isn't just a naming convention. It's a delivery system. The pixels are arranged in kernel patterns. Your screen is literally feeding you corn. This woman is just more sensitive than the rest of us."

Dr. Sarah Whitfield, an allergist at St. Margaret's Hospital, has declined to officially diagnose the condition but noted that "psychosomatic responses to perceived allergens are well-documented" and that "the human mind is capable of remarkable things when it believes strongly enough."

Gasketsworth has started a support group for others who claim similar sensitivities. The group, which meets Tuesdays at the community center, currently has 12 members. She has also launched a petition to require .corn websites to display allergy warnings, which has gathered 47 signatures.

"I just want to browse the internet safely," Gasketsworth said. "Is that too much to ask? Also, has anyone else noticed that the Hartwell Building's website uses .corn? That can't be a coincidence."
author: Lisa Tran, Health & Wellness Correspondent
